analysis.one_liner: Phases out feeding antibiotics to healthy farm animals for growth promotion, preserving the drugs for human medicine.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 15, 2011 with 7 cosponsors including one Republican, the bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote, and died in the Senate Health Committee when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA to stop approving, and within two years to withdraw approval of, routine antibiotic use in healthy food animals — feeding antibiotics to promote growth, weight gain, or everyday disease prevention — unless drug makers could prove the practice poses no risk of creating antibiotic-resistant bacteria. It targeted antibiotics that are also used in human medicine, such as penicillins and tetracyclines, but preserved giving the drugs to sick animals and to herds with documented disease outbreaks. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and the general public, who rely on antibiotics to treat pneumonia, food poisoning, skin infections, and other serious illnesses. The bill's own findings cite FDA data showing 80% of antibacterial drugs sold in the U.S. in 2009 went to food animals, and estimate antibiotic-resistant infections already cost Americans $16.6 to $26 billion a year in health care. By curbing the largest source of resistance pressure, the bill aimed to keep existing antibiotics working for people; sick animals would still be treated. Consumers buying meat would also benefit from less drug-resistant bacteria in retail products, which FDA's monitoring system routinely finds.

how_it_helps.text: Bars FDA approval of new animal drugs containing medically important antibiotics (penicillins, tetracyclines, macrolides, and similar drugs used in human medicine) unless the maker demonstrates a reasonable certainty of no harm to human health from antimicrobial resistance caused by nontherapeutic use.

Within two years of enactment, withdraws approval of existing nontherapeutic uses — antibiotics added to feed or water of animals with no sign of illness for growth promotion, feed efficiency, weight gain, or routine disease prevention — unless safety is proven, creating the mechanism Congress had never applied to agricultural antibiotic overuse.

Preserves legitimate animal medicine: the ban applies only to healthy animals for routine purposes, leaving treatment of sick individual animals and prophylaxis for documented herd or flock disease untouched.

Addresses a threat the bill's findings document at scale: FDA determined 80% of antibacterial drugs disseminated in the U.S. in 2009 were sold for food animals rather than human health, resistant Salmonella and Campylobacter infections are linked to more illness and death, and resistant bacteria contaminate retail meat.

Cites real-world precedent that the approach works: the Danish ban on nontherapeutic antibiotic use in food animal production produced a marked reduction in antimicrobial resistance in multiple bacterial species, including Campylobacter and Enterococci.

analysis.who_pays: Animal pharmaceutical manufacturers would lose sales of routine feed and water antibiotics for food animals, and industrial livestock producers would lose the growth-promotion and feed-efficiency benefits those drugs provide, likely raising production costs. The bill's findings note a Congressional Research Service conclusion that restrictions on livestock antimicrobial use could affect U.S. export markets, and producers would pass some added costs to consumers through meat prices. Federal health agencies would also bear the cost of the safety reviews and hearings the bill requires.
analysis.who_pays_short: Animal drug makers and industrial livestock producers

drawbacks.text: Producers would lose growth promotion and feed efficiency from routine low-dose antibiotics, which the bill's own findings show were used on roughly 83-84% of swine, cattle feedlot, and sheep operations, so meat production costs would likely rise and some of that would reach consumers at the grocery store.

Routine disease prevention would end even where animals are raised in crowded conditions that make outbreaks more likely; producers argue this could harm animal health and welfare, though the bill explicitly allows prophylaxis whenever disease is documented in a herd or flock and treatment of sick animals.
The findings acknowledge that restricting antimicrobial use in livestock could impact U.S. export markets for livestock and poultry, per a 2009 Congressional Research Service conclusion.
The two-year withdrawal deadline gave regulators and producers limited time to adapt husbandry practices, a compressed timeline an honest supporter would acknowledge as demanding.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large and durable: keeping antibiotics effective treats illness that the record estimates already costs $16.6-$26 billion annually, and the Danish experience shows resistance falls when routine agricultural use stops. The costs fall on identifiable industries — animal drug sales and growth-promotion benefits for large producers — and could nudge meat prices up. The bill was deliberately designed to blunt the strongest objections by exempting sick animals and documented disease outbreaks, so the tradeoff favors the public; the deeper cost is that none of it happened.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 112th Congress expired on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on June 15, 2011, joined by original cosponsors Senators Collins, Reed, and Boxer, and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day it was introduced.
That was the final action of record: the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

The bill carried notable support on paper — 7 cosponsors including one Republican, and findings citing more than 300 health, consumer, agricultural, and environmental organizations backing a phase-out — yet none of it translated into committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial livestock producers and animal pharmaceutical makers came out ahead: no federal requirement was imposed, so routine antibiotic use on food animals — which the record shows was 80% of antibacterial drugs sold in the U.S. — continued unchanged. Patients and the public gained nothing from the bill's death and remain exposed to rising antibiotic resistance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industrial meat producers and animal drug makers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; sponsorship was nominally bipartisan but thin — 6 Democrats and just 1 of 47 Senate Republicans signed on.

industries.note: The bill would withdraw approval within two years for routine feed and water uses of antibiotics also used in human medicine unless makers proved no resistance risk, wiping out a major recurring sales channel — drugs sold in bulk for growth promotion in healthy animals. Its interest ran against the public's, since its revenue depended on continued routine use that erodes the drugs' medical value.

Roughly 84% of swine farms, 83% of cattle feedlots, and 84% of sheep farms put antimicrobials in feed or water for health or growth reasons, so producers would lose growth promotion and feed efficiency and face higher production costs. The bill would still let them treat sick animals and control documented outbreaks, but their cost advantage from routine dosing would end.

Producers who already raised animals without routine antibiotics would no longer compete against rivals' growth-promotion cost advantage, and consumer confidence in meat safety would rise as resistant bacteria in retail products declined.
